metadata.methods_description: EEG recordings were conducted in a sound-isolating booth using a Brain Products system in BrainVision format. Stimuli were presented via ER-2 insert earphones for air conduction and a B-81 vibrator for bone conduction, controlled through an RME Digiface USB interface and custom Python scripts using expyfun. The pABR paradigm employed tone pips (500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000 Hz) presented at 40 Hz stimulation rate for air conduction (dichotic) and bone conduction (with contralateral masking at 400 Hz) across intensity levels of 20, 40, 50, 60, 70, and 30 dB peSPL. Behavioral data were collected using eye-tracking equipment with stimulus presentation rates of 20, 40, 60, and 80 Hz.

citation_details.title: The parallel auditory brainstem response paradigm provides accurate and fast hearing thresholds in a clinic-like setting
citation_details.author: Melissa J. Polonenko, Ross K. Maddox
citation_details.abstract: Objectives: The auditory brainstem response (ABR) is an essential tool in screening for and diagnosing infant hearing loss, and its results drive decisions regarding interventions and hearing habilitation with impacts extending far into a child's future. Despite the traditional ABR exam's usefulness, there is an identified need to develop faster, more informative exams. The parallel ABR (pABR) measures responses to all frequencies of interest in both ears all at once, rather than the traditional series of single-frequency measurements in one ear at a time, greatly speeding the diagnostic exam. The pABR has been shown to be effective at quickly measuring frequency-specific responses in adults with normal hearing, but it has not yet been tested in people with hearing loss. The goal of this study was to determine the accuracy and speed of the pABR for estimating hearing thresholds in a clinic-like setting. Design: Seventy adults with widely varying sensorineural hearing loss configuration
